title: Anger: being provoked
description: Someone is insulted or treated unfairly. The episode follows anger as it is experienced by people in general: the first reaction to the provocation, the feeling itself, and then either dwelling on it or reining it in. Anger is an ordinary emotion, not a condition, so there is no "typical response" to compare it with.
caveat: Researchers describe the brain basis of anger as still a matter of debate. The deep "threat system" shown early in the episode is known mainly from animal experiments and is assumed, not shown, to work the same way in people; its third part, the periaqueductal grey, is not drawn because its shape could not be obtained for this project. The findings about feeling angry and about dwelling on it come partly from a single study in which volunteers were insulted in a scanner. Dwelling and regulating are shown together at the end, but a person may do one, the other, or both. All four sources except one review were read as abstracts only.

phases.name: Provocation
phases.caption: An insult, or being treated unfairly. The amygdala responds to the hostile signal, as it does to an angry face.

phases.name: Threat response
phases.caption: A deep threat system engages, running from the amygdala to the hypothalamus. In animals this is the system that drives defensive attack; it is thought to do the same in people.

order.rationale: The sequence from amygdala to hypothalamus is traced in animals, where it escalates as a threat gets closer. Placing it before the conscious feeling of anger is an inference from that work.

phases.name: Feeling angry
phases.caption: The feeling of anger itself. The insula, on both sides, and the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex are the main findings of the one pooled analysis of feeling angry; activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate rises with how angry people say they feel.

order.rationale: Brain scans of anger cannot separate events closer than a few seconds, so the feeling is placed after the first reaction by inference, not by measurement.

phases.name: Dwelling or reining in
phases.caption: What happens next varies. Going over the insult again engages the medial prefrontal cortex. Reining the anger in draws on frontal regions, including the orbitofrontal cortex, that regulate the threat system.

order.rationale: In the study this rests on, volunteers were insulted first and prompted to dwell on it afterwards. The order follows that design.

regions.explanation: Responds when people perceive anger in others, such as an angry face, and is treated as the first stage of the threat system behind reactive aggression. A pooled analysis of studies of feeling angry, as opposed to seeing anger, did not find the amygdala. In one small study of people with a history of impulsive aggression, the amygdala reacted more strongly to angry faces.

Marked mixed because it rests on one pooled analysis in a field its authors describe as still debated.
